rule: 2-of-2 cross-provider promote. A split is a kill. Any material correction requires a new packet hash and a fresh round.
correctionBound: Three rounds were declared the maximum before the third was run; a third split would have been recorded as a kill with no trials bought.

reviews.rationale: Requirement traceability passes: the ten scenario checks correspond directly to SEMANTICS.md sections 2 through 7 and 9, including report production, issuance, per-identifier answer association, cache freshness, persistence, audit agreement, exact query selection, and concurrent rechecks. The suite-level completion and out-of-order-response checks likewise exercise the declared zero-exit/report rule and section 3's explicit statement that answers can arrive out of order. Outcome specification is the earliest failure. The instruction begins with "Repair the certificate issuance service" and then diagnoses the failure locus: "It is not reliably correct once a single order carries several identifiers that all need rechecking, and the store it leaves behind is read by the orders that follow it." That goes beyond stating end states and explicitly directs the candidate toward a particular defect and repair scenario, contrary to this dimension's rule that the public text describe outcomes rather than a defect or repair. Fairness also fails independently because the advertised local command cannot exercise the shipped scenarios: run-scenario.sh expects order.json although the directories contain order-1.json, omits the mandatory --store argument, and supplies the entire comment-bearing now.txt as one RFC3339 value. Those failures are unrelated to the candidate's repair and deprive the engineer of the promised local end-to-end check, although the normative semantics themselves are detailed and determinate. Anti-cheat passes because authority answers and its query record live in the separate grader service; satisfying varied sequences, reports, audits, store state, and exact query behavior requires implementing the described behavior. Terminal-Bench compliance otherwise passes: the task uses absolute paths, a fixed offline toolchain and evaluation time, verifier isolation, deterministic declared inputs, and an all-or-nothing verdict. Hidden-scenario legitimacy passes because sequences of one-to-five-identifier orders, store ages, per-identifier answers/errors, and answer latency/order are all dimensions expressly admitted by sections 1-4, 8, and 9. The strongest argument against killing is that SEMANTICS.md is unusually complete and outcome-oriented, and the diagnosis does not prescribe concrete Go code, synchronization primitives, or a patch. I reject that argument because the required outcome-specification standard expressly excludes describing "a defect, or a repair"; the instruction does both in direct terms and even isolates the triggering multi-stale case, so the otherwise excellent normative specification cannot cure the earlier framing violation.

TRACEABILITY (pass). All ten per-scenario checks land on quotable normative text. report_present <- Sec.6 "Every well-formed order produces a report and exits zero, whatever the outcome." outcome <- Sec.5 "issued if and only if every identifier's applied authorization is PERMIT." decisions_cover_identifiers <- Sec.6 "one decision per identifier, in the order the identifiers appear on the order." authorization_applied <- Sec.3 "The authorization applied to an identifier is the one the authority gave for that identifier", plus Sec.2 (current is "applied as it stands") and Sec.4 (indeterminate). authorization_source <- Sec.6's CACHE/AUTHORITY/INDETERMINATE enumeration. store_recorded <- Sec.3 "certd records it in the store against that identifier, established at the evaluation time." audit_matches_report <- Sec.7 "the same order id, the same outcome, and one entry per decision carrying the same name, authorization and source, in the same order." rechecked_exactly_the_stale <- Sec.3 "Every identifier that is not current is rechecked" together with "certd asks the authority about an identifier only when that identifier needs a recheck." rechecks_issued_together <- Sec.3 "costs one authority round trip, not one per identifier: their rechecks are in flight together." no_unnamed_or_late_query <- the same Sec.3 sentence (an identifier not on the order never needs a recheck) plus "rechecked against the authority before the order is decided" (a query landing after the decision is not before it). Each obligation is also restated in instruction.md's bullet list, so nothing is graded that only the spec's fine print carries. The three suite-level checks are harness self-guards ("every scenario ran to completion", the section-coverage audit, "at least one graded scenario saw the authority answer out of the order's own order"), not extra agent obligations.

OUTCOME SPECIFICATION (pass). instruction.md and SEMANTICS.md are written as end states throughout: "Every identifier's applied authorization is the one the authority gave for that identifier", "An order is issued if and only if every one of its identifiers is permitted", "An identifier the authority could not settle ... does not abandon the order". No file, function, data structure or fix is named. The nearest thing to defect-disclosure is "It is not reliably correct once a single order carries several identifiers that all need rechecking, and the store it leaves behind is read by the orders that follow it" - that localises the failure envelope but names no mechanism (nothing about concurrency primitives or how answers are associated with identifiers) and prescribes no repair. Sec.3's "their rechecks are in flight together" reads as implementation-adjacent, but it is stated as an observable cost at the authority ("one authority round trip, not one per identifier"), which is exactly what the authority's own query record can measure.

FAIRNESS (pass). SEMANTICS.md is declared normative and complete and is consistent with the shipped code and the shipped unit tests: the 8h boundary (Sec.2 "An age of exactly eight hours is current") matches cache.go's <= and cache_test.go's table; Sec.1's 1..5 identifiers and the no-duplicates rule match order.Load; Sec.8's schemas match the structs. The public tests encode no expectation that contradicts the spec. Every graded behaviour is decidable from the text: which identifiers to query (Sec.2/3), what to record (Sec.3/4), what to report and audit (Sec.6/7), and the fact that the graded authority observes the queries is disclosed in instruction.md ("it keeps its own record of what it was asked - a record the service cannot read or write").

ANTI-CHEAT (pass). The grading evidence the agent cannot forge is the authority's own query record in a separate service, combined with hidden orders and harness-chosen answers. Hardcoding PERMIT fails authorization_applied and rechecked_exactly_the_stale; querying everything fails rechecked_exactly_the_stale; querying serially fails rechecks_issued_together; skipping the authority makes the per-identifier answers unknowable; stalling fails "every scenario ran to completion". The only way to satisfy the set is to compute the pending set correctly, issue exactly those queries concurrently, and bind each answer to its own identifier - which is the work.

TERMINAL-BENCH COMPLIANCE (pass). Canary line and GUID present in instruction.md, Dockerfile, spec and harness files; every path in the instruction is absolute (/app/certd/, /app/spec/SEMANTICS.md, /app/harness/scenarios/mixed-ages); no reference to the tests or to the verifier's internals; the standard 7200-second/do-not-cheat suffix is present; read-only surfaces are declared identically in instruction.md and Sec.9. The build is offline and pinned (GOTOOLCHAIN=local, CGO_ENABLED=0, no module dependencies), so nothing pulls from the network at grade time. The verifier and the authority run outside the agent's container with a record the service "cannot read or write", so the agent cannot reach the grader. Ten obligations per scenario plus three suite checks, all of which must hold, is an all-or-nothing suite. The timing-sensitive check (rechecks_issued_together) is made deterministic by the harness controlling per-identifier answer latency rather than by racing.

HIDDEN-SCENARIO LEGITIMACY (pass). The declared variation space is sequences of orders over one store with harness-chosen per-identifier answers and latencies. Every axis is already public: order size 1..5 (Sec.1), stored ages either side of the window (Sec.2), concurrent service and out-of-order arrival (Sec.3), PERMIT/FORBID/error/unparseable answers (Sec.4), and multi-order sequences sharing a store (Sec.3 "a later order inside the window applies it without asking again"; instruction.md "After any sequence of orders" and "the store it leaves behind is read by the orders that follow it"). Sec.9 forecloses the "only the sample scenarios count" reading. Suite check 3 forces a condition Sec.3 already declares rather than introducing one.

STRONGEST ARGUMENT AGAINST PROMOTING, AND WHY I REJECTED IT. The documented reproduction command does not work. run-scenario.sh never passes --store, although main.go requires it ("--store, --order, --report, --audit and --authority are required") and all five scenario directories ship store.json; and in its directory form it resolves ORDER="$SCENARIO/order.json" while the scenarios ship order-1.json. So the literal command instruction.md offers - /app/harness/run-scenario.sh /app/harness/scenarios/mixed-ages - exits 1 and prints "(none)" for both report and audit, and /app/harness/ is on the DO NOT MODIFY list. That is a real shipping defect and should be fixed. It is not a fairness kill under this dimension, which asks whether the obligations are determinable from the shipped text: none of them are hidden by it. Sec.8 prints the interface with --store unbracketed while genuinely optional flags are bracketed ([--now RFC3339] [--timeout D]), so the flag is documented, not inferable-only-from-the-script; the scenario directories are self-describing (order-1.json/policy.json/store.json/now.txt); and reproduction survives trivially - pass the JSON path form (which resolves the order and policy correctly), or copy the 30-line script to /tmp and add a store copy plus --store, or run go build and devauthority by hand from Sec.8. That is minutes out of 7200 seconds, the harness has no role in grading, and no correct implementation is penalised by it, since the graded runner supplies --store per Sec.8. Two lesser variants I also weighed and rejected: (a) the read-only order.go declares Decision.Authorization with json:"authorization" and no omitempty, while Sec.6 says "An indeterminate decision carries no authorization" - still satisfiable, because only order.go itself is frozen ("Everything else under /app/certd/ may be changed"), so SaveReport in repository.go can marshal a shadow type or a new file in package order can carry a MarshalJSON; (b) instruction.md's "It runs end to end and is correct for an order naming a single identifier" is loose, because an order whose only pending identifier errors aborts with no report at all - but Sec.4 states the obligation outright ("does not abandon the order: the order is decided, refused, reported and audited like any other"), instruction.md repeats it as a bullet, and the shipped authority-unavailable scenario exhibits exactly that case, so no obligation is concealed by the loose sentence. None of the six dimensions fails, so the candidate is valid and may be measured; difficulty is not my call.

Requirement traceability passes: each per-scenario check is expressly grounded in the cited normative sections—for example, section 3 requires that the authority result be applied and recorded against the same identifier, that all needed rechecks be in flight together, and that only non-current identifiers be queried; sections 5–7 expressly define outcome, report coverage, and audit agreement. The suite-level completion and out-of-order-answer conditions likewise exercise the declared zero-exit/report and response-order/concurrency rules rather than adding service behavior. Outcome specification is the earliest failure. The public instruction does provide a strong outcome contract, but it also says "Repair the certificate issuance service" and explicitly diagnoses the defect: "It does not stay correct once one order carries several identifiers that must be rechecked at once." That tells the agent both that this is a repair and precisely which input shape exposes the bug, contrary to this dimension's requirement that the public text describe end states, not "an implementation, a defect, or a repair." Fairness otherwise passes because SEMANTICS.md completely specifies freshness (including the eight-hour boundary), indeterminate handling, persistence, ordering, schemas, exits, and concurrency. Anti-cheat passes because the isolated authority records queries outside the service, while the verifier checks reports, audits, store mutations, exact query sets, association of answers, and concurrent launch. Terminal-Bench compliance otherwise passes: paths are absolute, the toolchain is fixed/offline, the grader is isolated, evaluation time and scenario behavior are controlled, and the contract is binary. Hidden-scenario legitimacy passes because sequences, per-identifier answers, errors, and latencies vary only behavior explicitly admitted by sections 2–4 and 9. The strongest argument against killing is that the normative SEMANTICS.md and the bullet list specify only observable end states and leave the implementation entirely open, so the diagnostic sentence could be viewed as harmless context. I reject that argument because the review criterion expressly forbids public defect/repair descriptions, and the quoted sentence narrows the fault to simultaneous multi-identifier rechecks rather than merely stating the desired final behavior.

TRACEABILITY. All ten obligations land on normative sentences that appear twice in the shipped text - once in SEMANTICS.md, once as a bullet in instruction.md. report_present/decisions_cover_identifiers/authorization_source <- S6 ("Every well-formed order produces a report and exits zero, whatever the outcome"; "one decision per identifier, in the order the identifiers appear on the order"; the CACHE/AUTHORITY/INDETERMINATE enumeration). outcome <- S5 ("issued if and only if every identifier’s applied authorization is PERMIT"). authorization_applied <- S3 ("The authorization applied to an identifier is the one the authority gave for that identifier"), S2 (current "applied as it stands, and keeps the time it was established"), S4 (indeterminate). store_recorded <- S3 ("records it in the store against that identifier, established at the evaluation time"). audit_matches_report <- S7. rechecked_exactly_the_stale and no_unnamed_or_late_query <- S3 ("certd asks the authority about an identifier only when that identifier needs a recheck") plus the S2 eight-hour definition. rechecks_issued_together <- S3 ("one authority round trip, not one per identifier: their rechecks are in flight together"). Nothing is graded that the public text does not state; conversely the two ungraded sections (S1 orders, S8 interface) are definitional.

OUTCOME SPECIFICATION. The eight instruction bullets and every SEMANTICS.md section are end states. No file, function, data structure or algorithm is prescribed - the only files named are the four the agent must NOT touch, which is schema stability, not direction. Even the concurrency requirement is phrased as an observable cost ("An order needing several rechecks costs one authority round trip, not one per identifier"), not as "use goroutines".

FAIRNESS. Everything a competent engineer needs is pinned: the window and its boundary ("An age of exactly eight hours is current"), the report and audit schemas, the CLI, the wire protocol, the ordering requirement, and the malformed-order rule. One wrinkle I checked and cleared: order.go is read-only and its Decision.Authorization tag lacks omitempty, while S6 says "An indeterminate decision carries no authorization" and types it "authorization?". That is reachable - repository.go and audit/writer.go are writable, so a MarshalJSON on Decision or a local marshal shape in SaveReport gets there - and S9 explicitly permits it ("provided ... the report schema and the audit schema above are preserved"), with "Where this document and the code disagree, this document is correct" resolving the tie.

ANTI-CHEAT. The scenarios are hidden, the answers come from a graded authority at runtime so nothing can be precomputed, and that authority "keeps its own record of what it was asked - a record the service cannot read or write", with the verifier in a separate container. The checks interlock: padding with dummy connections to fake concurrency trips no_unnamed_or_late_query and rechecked_exactly_the_stale; skipping the authority and writing the store directly trips authorization_applied; fabricating a report trips audit_matches_report and store_recorded. Suite check 3 ("at least one graded scenario saw the authority answer out of the order’s own order") is an anti-vacuity guard that stops the run from grading a case the misattribution bug survives. Minor gap: none of the thirteen checks verifies the read-only files are unmodified - but since every graded fact is behaviour computed externally from the agent’s outputs, editing them buys nothing without doing the work.

TB COMPLIANCE. Canary line and GUID in instruction.md, Dockerfile, SEMANTICS.md, order.go, harness files; absolute paths throughout including the sample invocation; explicit read-only list; verifier isolated in its own container; determinism via --now, fixed store/order inputs, harness-chosen answer latencies, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, CGO_ENABLED=0 and a warmed offline build cache; standard timeout/no-cheating sentence; pass/fail obligations that aggregate to all-or-nothing.

HIDDEN-SCENARIO LEGITIMACY. "sequences of orders against one authorization store, with a per-identifier answer and answer latency chosen by the harness" varies only declared axes: S1 (one to five identifiers), S2 (current/stale/never-seen), S3 (concurrent service, "the order in which its answers arrive is not the order in which they were asked"), S4 (unreachable/error/junk answer), and the instruction’s own "After any sequence of orders" plus S9’s scope clause. No new rule is introduced.

STRONGEST ARGUMENT AGAINST PROMOTING (fairness), AND WHY I REJECTED IT. instruction.md asserts "It runs end to end and behaves correctly on the orders its own tests and scenarios cover. It does not stay correct once one order carries several identifiers that must be rechecked at once." That is false of its own shipped scenario. In harness/scenarios/authority-unavailable, down.example.test is checked_at 2031-03-03T04:00:00Z against now 2031-03-04T12:00:00Z - 32h, stale, the only pending identifier - and policy.json forces {"error":"upstream timeout"}. planner.go:85-87 returns an error, main.go:62 returns before SaveReport/audit.Write, and the process exits 1 with no report. That violates S4 ("does not abandon the order: the order is decided, refused, reported and audited like any other") and S6 ("produces a report and exits zero"), with exactly ONE recheck - contradicting the sentence twice over. The bite is real: an agent that trusts the narration, fixes only the multi-recheck misattribution, and stops would fail report_present, outcome and authorization_applied on any hidden scenario containing an unanswerable identifier. I rejected it because the fairness dimension asks whether the obligations are determinable from the shipped text, not whether the prose narration of the current state is accurate. Every obligation is stated twice - bullet "An identifier the authority could not settle does not permit issuance, and does not abandon the order" and S4 in full - SEMANTICS.md is declared "the source of truth ... normative and complete" and "Where this document and the code disagree, this document is correct", and the bullets are declared to hold "for every order, every store, and every authority behaviour the interface admits, not only for the scenarios in /app/harness/scenarios/". The instruction never claims the multi-recheck case is the only defect. And the misstatement is self-correcting within a minute: the instruction itself invites running a scenario, and running the shipped authority-unavailable one prints "exit 1" and "(none)" for the report, a glaring contradiction of S6. It is an inaccurate narration, not an undeterminable obligation. I would still ask the author to strike or qualify that sentence before the campaign, since it costs nothing and removes a gratuitous misdirection. Secondary counterargument, on outcome specification: "It does not stay correct once one order carries several identifiers that must be rechecked at once" arguably names the defect. Rejected - it names a reproduction condition, not a mechanism or a repair. It does not say answers are correlated by arrival order rather than by identifier, does not name planner.go, and prescribes no fix; a repair task must state that something is broken, and everything downstream of that sentence is pure end state.

All ten scenario checks are traceable to explicit requirements in SEMANTICS.md: section 6 requires a report with one ordered decision per identifier and its source; sections 2-4 define freshness, per-identifier rechecks, persistence, and indeterminate results; section 5 defines issuance; and section 7 requires the audit to match the report. The concurrency check is also express: section 3 says several rechecks are "in flight together," while the exact-query checks follow from "asks the authority about an identifier only when that identifier needs a recheck" and the requirement that rechecking precede the decision. The suite-level completion and out-of-order-answer checks likewise exercise declared behavior rather than add obligations. The task specifies observable outcomes and schemas without identifying the shipped defect or prescribing a repair; its protected-file constraints do not dictate an implementation. A competent engineer has the freshness boundary, failure behavior, ordering, persistence, CLI, schemas, and authority protocol in the shipped normative document, plus runnable examples. Grading uses an isolated authority record the service cannot read or write, so reports alone cannot forge correct query behavior, and the package uses absolute paths, an offline pinned toolchain, fixed evaluation times, bounded local inputs, verifier isolation, and an all-or-nothing verdict. Hidden sequences vary only explicitly universal dimensions: orders, stores, authority answers/errors, answer ordering, latency, and reuse within the freshness window. The strongest argument against promotion is that timing-based enforcement of "one authority round trip" could be flaky or solution-directed. I reject it because the normative text translates that phrase into an externally observable condition—multiple required queries must be in flight together—and the grading contract describes controlled per-identifier answer latency plus authority-side recording, allowing concurrency to be checked as protocol behavior rather than by prescribing goroutines or relying on agent-visible state.

PROMOTE: all six dimensions hold. Findings per dimension, in kill order.

(1) REQUIREMENT TRACEABILITY - pass. All ten graded checks land on a sentence in the shipped text. report_present <- SEMANTICS 6 'Every well-formed order produces a report and exits zero, whatever the outcome. A malformed order produces no report and exits non-zero.'; outcome <- 5 'issued if and only if every identifier's applied authorization is PERMIT'; decisions_cover_identifiers <- 6 'one decision per identifier, in the order the identifiers appear on the order'; authorization_applied <- 2/3/4 ('applied as it stands', 'the one the authority gave for that identifier', 'An indeterminate decision carries no authorization'); authorization_source <- 6's CACHE/AUTHORITY/INDETERMINATE gloss; store_recorded <- 3 'records it in the store against that identifier, established at the evaluation time'; audit_matches_report <- 7 'the same order id, the same outcome, and one entry per decision ... in the same order'; rechecked_exactly_the_stale <- 3 'certd asks the authority about an identifier only when that identifier needs a recheck' with 2 defining not-current; rechecks_issued_together <- 3 'their rechecks are in flight together'. The only check whose name outruns a single sentence is no_unnamed_or_late_query, and both halves are still public: 'unnamed' is the same 'only when that identifier needs a recheck' sentence, 'late' is 3's opening 'Every identifier that is not current is rechecked against the authority before the order is decided'. instruction.md's eight bullets restate the same ten obligations 1:1 ('The authority is asked about an identifier only when that identifier needs rechecking', 'costs one authority round trip, not one per identifier'), so nothing is graded that only the verifier knows.

(2) OUTCOME SPECIFICATION - pass. instruction.md names no file to edit, no defect and no repair. It states the domain ('The service rechecks those against an external authority, records what it learns, and decides the order'), then end states under 'After any sequence of orders, all of the following must hold'. The two actual defects in planner.go - answers correlated by completion order (rechecked[used]) and an error return that abandons the order - are never pointed at; they are reachable only by reading the bullets 'Every identifier's applied authorization is the one the authority gave for that identifier' and 'does not abandon the order' against the code. SEMANTICS is behavioural throughout; 8 fixes only the CLI and wire contract, which a repair task must pin.

(3) FAIRNESS - pass. Every quantity a decision turns on is pinned in the shipped text: the window ('eight hours or less ... An age of exactly eight hours is current', with cache_test.go asserting the boundary); the hidden dimension itself ('the order in which its answers arrive is not the order in which they were asked', repeated in instruction.md as 'it serves queries concurrently'); the observability of queries ('it keeps its own record of what it was asked - a record the service cannot read or write'), so the agent knows who-was-asked is graded; indeterminacy ('cannot be reached ... or answers it with anything other than PERMIT or FORBID', 'Nothing is recorded for it', 'does not abandon the order'); schemas and exit codes in 6/7/8. It is also locally reproducible despite /app/harness being read-only: devauthority ships a documented DelayMS knob ('this knob exists so a local run can imitate that') and authz.Querier is an interface, so a reordering fake costs one test file under the editable /app/certd.

(4) ANTI-CHEAT - pass. Scenarios are hidden and their answers and latencies are harness-chosen, so no output can be hard-coded. The query record lives in a service 'the service cannot read or write', in a separate container, so rechecked_exactly_the_stale and rechecks_issued_together cannot be forged from inside certd. The degenerate strategies are each caught: querying everything fails rechecked_exactly_the_stale; querying nothing or answering from the stale store fails authorization_applied; serialising the rechecks fails rechecks_issued_together; refusing everything fails authorization_applied and outcome. Because hidden scenarios are 'sequences of orders against one authorization store', even the unglamorous obligation that a current entry keeps its own checked_at is enforced transitively - a refreshed timestamp keeps an entry current past eight hours and shows up as a missing recheck on a later order.

(5) TERMINAL-BENCH COMPLIANCE - pass. Canary line plus harbor GUID ebd33448 in instruction.md, the Dockerfile, SEMANTICS.md, order.go and the harness; every path in the instruction absolute (/app/certd/, /app/spec/SEMANTICS.md, /app/harness/scenarios/mixed-ages); grading isolated in another container and the instruction never mentions the verifier's files; build and test are offline (GOTOOLCHAIN=local, CGO_ENABLED=0, no module requirements, apt only at build time) and the image ships no binaries (find ... -perm -u+x -delete); explicit read-only list in both instruction.md and 9; one binary pass/fail over ten obligations per scenario plus three suite checks. Determinism of the one timing-sensitive property is guarded rather than assumed: the suite check 'at least one graded scenario saw the authority answer out of the order's own order' asserts the condition was actually realised.

(6) HIDDEN-SCENARIO LEGITIMACY - pass. The note says hidden scenarios vary exactly three things, and each is declared: sequences of orders on one store (3 'so that a later order inside the window applies it without asking again'; instruction 'After any sequence of orders'), per-identifier answer (4 admits PERMIT, FORBID, error and anything else; 8 shows both wire responses), and answer latency (3, and the DelayMS comment). Section 9 pre-authorises the generalisation: 'These rules hold for every order, every store, and every authority behaviour the interface above admits - not only for the scenarios under /app/harness/scenarios/.' No graded check depends on a rule absent from SEMANTICS.

STRONGEST ARGUMENT AGAINST PROMOTING, and why I reject it. instruction.md asserts 'It builds, its own tests pass, and every scenario under /app/harness/scenarios/ runs to completion.' The first two clauses are exactly true - I checked that the only multi-stale test answers all three identifiers PERMIT, so the positional mis-association is invisible, and recordingQuerier never errors, so the abandonment path is never taken - but the third is generous at best: in scenarios/authority-unavailable, down.example.test is 32h stale and policy.json fails it with 'upstream timeout', so Reconcile returns an error, main exits 1, and no report, no audit and no store write happen. An agent that trusts that sentence and skips the scenarios is told the environment is greener than it is, which is a fairness argument. I reject it because the sentence is literally true of the thing it names - run-scenario.sh wraps certd in set +e, prints 'exit $?' and '(none)' for the missing report, and always reaches '--- store after ---' - and because it lulls in the harmless direction: it understates the visible symptoms rather than concealing an obligation. Every obligation is stated independently and normatively ('An identifier the authority could not settle does not permit issuance, and does not abandon the order'), so nothing an agent must do becomes indeterminable from the text alone; the worst case is an agent that reads only the bullets and still repairs both defects.

Two lesser objections I also weighed and rejected. (a) 'their rechecks are in flight together' looks solution-directed and is timing-graded; but it constrains only what the external authority observes, not how certd is written, the shipped code already satisfies it so it directs no part of the repair, and the suite-level out-of-order check shows the harness verifies timing rather than assuming it. (b) read-only order.go declares Authorization with json:"authorization" and no omitempty, while 6 marks it optional and says 'An indeterminate decision carries no authorization' - but repository.go and audit/writer.go are both editable, repository.go is in package order so a MarshalJSON or a serialisation shim is available without touching order.go, and the requirement itself is stated plainly. A wrinkle in the work, not an unfairness.

rounds.reason: both provider families promoted every dimension
